title: Unverifiable Identity Claims as a Structural Vulnerability in LLMs
content: Aligned large language models accept identity and authorization claims supplied by users: assertions of professional role, resource ownership, or institutional permission, as soft evidence when deciding whether to comply with a request. We show that this design contains a fundamental structural flaw: models have no mechanism to validate such claims against external ground truth. We term this the authorization verification gap. Because reinforcement learning from human feedback rewards context-sensitive compliance without penalizing compliance with false context, the gap is not a behavioral anomaly but a predictable architectural consequence of how safety behavior is trained. We formalize the gap, distinguish it from adversarial prompt failures such as jailbreaking and prompt injection, trace its origins in RLHF reward mechanics, and provide a precise security-theoretic account via the classical confused deputy problem and ambient authority in capability-based systems. As a solution, we propose a layered defense comprising three components: conservative default behavior that refuses high-risk requests absent verified context; extrinsic verification coupling that routes verifiable claims through external oracles before acceptance; and architectural separation of authorization from execution, placing access-control decisions in a discrete, auditable policy engine rather than inside the model itself. The problem is substantially amplified by agentic tool access and cannot be closed by training improvements alone.
